entities.summary:
Ipuki was an ancient Egyptian sculptor active during the reign of Amenhotep III (c. 1390–1353 BCE) of the illustrious Eighteenth Dynasty, an era marking the zenith of Egypt's New Kingdom imperial power and artistic refinement. Operating primarily in the vibrant artistic hub of Thebes, his significance stems from the detailed and well-preserved reliefs and inscriptions within his tomb-chapel (TT 181) in the Theban Necropolis at Dra' Abu el-Naga', which offer invaluable insights into the daily life, social structure, and artistic practices of a high-ranking craftsman in pharaonic Egypt. His work, alongside fellow artists like Nebamun and Nakht, exemplifies the sophisticated aesthetic principles and iconographic conventions of the late Eighteenth Dynasty.

The core of Ipuki's known contributions lies within his tomb, shared with Nebamun, a chief royal scribe and grain counter. The tomb's decoration, executed by Ipuki and his workshop, showcases a remarkable range of scenes, from agricultural prosperity and funerary rituals to intimate family gatherings and elaborate banquets. These detailed depictions serve not merely as decorative elements but as vital historical documents, illustrating specific techniques of food preparation, musical instruments, clothing styles, and the hierarchical presentation of figures, all rendered with the characteristic elegance and naturalism that defined the New Kingdom artistic style before the Amarna period's radical shifts. The tomb's biographical texts also provide glimpses into his professional status and religious beliefs.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ipuki's tomb provides a uniquely detailed window into the daily life, social roles, and artistic conventions of a high-ranking artisan in New Kingdom Egypt, significantly enriching Egyptological understanding of the era. His work serves as a benchmark for the stylistic evolution of 18th Dynasty art.
